paras: The lynching of William Allen was the hanging of a Black prisoner by a party of masked men near Warwick Court House, Virginia, on the night of December 5, 1881. Allen had been jailed three days earlier, accused of fatally stabbing a white man, William S. Selater, near Newport News. The lynchers reportedly obtained him with a forged transfer order, and the one man arrested, a white barber named Thomas Valentine, was discharged for lack of evidence.

A Fortress Monroe wire of December 3 reported that Selater, who lived on the Bowman Farm four miles north of Newport News, had been stabbed through the heart the night before by "a negro named William Allen." A Norfolk telegram to the Richmond Dispatch named them "Lem. Selater" and "George Allen" and said they had quarreled over a canoe.

The New York Sun's Fortress Monroe correspondent offered a fuller and different account on December 6. In it, two railroad workers named Kelly, who shared a house with Selater, hired Allen's mule to pull their wagon, and Allen resented Selater for accusing him of stealing an axe. On Friday evening Allen refused to let his mule pull the wagon with Selater in it, drove ahead after an argument, and stabbed Selater three times when he walked home. The Kellys seized Allen, and he was committed to the county jail at Warwick Court House.

On December 6 Henry Jones, "a prominent citizen of Warwick county," reached Hampton and reported that masked men had taken Allen from the jail the night before and hanged him "to a tree by the roadside." The wire version, opening "It is reported," said only that masked men had taken him from the jail and hanged him.

According to the Wilmington, Delaware, Daily Gazette, "a party of Sclater's friends" came to the jailer on the night of the 5th with a forged mittimus, purportedly from Justice Post, ordering Allen moved to a jail in an adjoining county. The jailer, supposing the order genuine, handed Allen over, and the men took him about a mile from the jail and lynched him. The Richmond Dispatch likewise said the order, sending Allen to Hampton, was forged so the lynchers "might get hold of the prisoner with less trouble."

The Gazette reported that none of the participants were known to the authorities. Even so, on December 14 Constable Harris of Elizabeth City County arrested Thomas Valentine, a white Richmond barber, on a warrant charging him with being one of the lynchers. He had kept a barbershop in Hampton at the time. At an examination in Hampton on December 20 he was discharged, "there being no evidence whatever against him."
No report of an inquest, a grand jury inquiry or any other arrest appears in the coverage.

Papers treated Allen's guilt as settled though he had not been tried: the Richmond Dispatch headlined "A Colored Murderer Lynched," the Wilmington Gazette "Lynching of a Negro Murderer." The New York Sun headed its story "A Mule Dispute, Murder, and Lynching"; none of the articles commented on the lynching itself.

Within two days the Fortress Monroe wire had run in Lancaster, Knoxville, Washington and Waco, and shorter notes followed in weeklies. Several briefs garbled the place: the Portland Daily Press put it at "Warwick, Vt.," the Waco paper at "Clarkville courthouse," and the St. Landry Democrat at Norfolk.

Valentine's arrest set off a second round of wire copies ("A Suspected Lyncher Arrested" in Savannah, "Arrested as a Lyncher" in Staunton), still running in the Somerset Herald on December 28. His discharge drew far less notice, appearing in the Richmond Dispatch and the Alexandria Gazette.

The Hampton report of December 6 and the Wilmington Gazette put the lynching on the night of the 5th, but a wire dated December 7 also said "last night." The first reports said masked men took Allen out of the jail, whereas the later Wilmington and Richmond accounts said the jailer released him on a forged order. The Evening Star, quoting the Richmond State, placed "the party of lynchers in Elizabeth City county," but the Hampton report of Valentine's discharge said Warwick County.

reader.title: Lynching of William Allen
bases: A party of masked men took William Allen, held in the Warwick county jail on a murder charge, and hanged him to a roadside tree (A5, A9, A15).

Allen was hanged without trial by 'a party of masked men', described as 'a party of Sclater's friends', who obtained him from the jailer with a forged order (A9, A15, A18); he was killed in reprisal for the stabbing of Selater, and every report calls it a lynching (A11, A15, A19). The papers give no number, but a 'party' of men implies more than two.

A Hampton report through Henry Jones (A9), the Associated Press wire from Fortress Monroe (A11), the fuller Wilmington Gazette account (A15) and the Richmond reports of Valentine's arrest and discharge (A18, A30) agree that Allen was taken from the Warwick jail and lynched.

framing.detail: The Richmond Dispatch headlined 'A Colored Murderer Lynched' and 'The Sequel of the Bowman-Farm Murder,' treating Allen's guilt as settled without comment on the lynching.
The Wilmington Gazette ran 'Lynching of a Negro Murderer' and described the forged mittimus without condemnation.
Most papers printed the one-sentence Fortress Monroe wire describing Allen as the man 'who killed' Selater, some misplacing it in Vermont, 'Clarkville' or Norfolk.
The Valentine arrest went out as a Richmond wire under headings such as 'A Suspected Lyncher Arrested' and 'Arrested as a Lyncher'.
